n: Paul opens his letter to the Corinthian saints the way ancient letters began — with the sender’s name. He reminds them that his apostleship came from God’s will, not his own ambition, and includes Sosthenes, a fellow believer.

f.g: Greek apostolos — one who is sent out with authority as a messenger.

n: The letter is addressed to the Church in Corinth, a wealthy, worldly port city in Greece. Paul calls them people made holy through Christ and called to be saints — together with believers everywhere.

f.g: A large Roman colony and trading center in southern Greece, known for wealth and loose morals.
Made holy, set apart for God.

n: Paul’s standard blessing joins the Greek greeting (grace) and the Hebrew greeting (peace), both flowing from the Father and the Son.

f.w: Grace be unto you, and peace

n: Though Paul will correct the Corinthians sharply, he starts with sincere gratitude for the grace God has given them through Jesus Christ.

f.g: God’s freely given help, favor, and enabling power through Christ.

n: Christ has made them rich in spiritual gifts — especially in speaking and in knowledge, two areas the Corinthians prized highly (and sometimes misused).

f.g: Speech — the ability to express spiritual truth, including gifts like tongues and prophecy.

n: These gifts were evidence that the testimony of Christ Paul preached had taken root among them and been confirmed by the Spirit.
They lacked no spiritual gift while they waited for the Second Coming. Early saints lived with eager expectation of the Lord’s return.

f.g: Fall short in no gift; lack nothing.

n: Christ will keep them strong to the end so they can stand blameless at his coming — a promise that rests on his power, not their perfection.

f.w: the day of our Lord Jesus Christ
f.g: The day of His Second Coming and judgment.

n: God keeps His promises. He invited them into fellowship — a shared life and partnership — with His Son.

f.g: Greek koinonia — sharing, communion, partnership.

n: Now Paul turns to the main problem: division. He pleads with them to be unified — to speak with one voice and share one mind and purpose, like a torn net mended back together.

f.g: Greek katartizo — to mend or restore, as fishermen repaired nets.

n: Members of Chloe’s household — perhaps her servants or family traveling on business — had reported to Paul that the Corinthian saints were quarreling.
The saints had formed fan clubs around leaders: some followed Paul, some Apollos, some Peter, and some proudly claimed only Christ. Rivalry had replaced unity.

f.g: An eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who taught in Corinth after Paul.
The Aramaic name of Peter, meaning “rock.”

n: Paul’s sharp questions expose the absurdity: Christ cannot be split into pieces. Paul was not crucified for them, and they were not baptized into Paul’s name but Christ’s.
Given the factions, Paul is glad he personally baptized very few of them — Crispus, the former synagogue ruler, and Gaius.
That way no one could claim they belonged to Paul because he baptized them. Baptism binds us to Christ, not to the person who performs it.
Paul corrects himself: he also baptized Stephanas’s household. Beyond that he can’t recall — the point is that who baptized whom doesn’t matter.
Paul’s main assignment was to preach, not to perform baptisms himself. He deliberately avoided impressive rhetoric so that the power of Christ’s cross, not his eloquence, would convert people.

f.g: Clever, polished speech — the trained rhetoric Greeks admired.
Emptied of its power.

n: To those headed for destruction, a message about a crucified Savior sounds foolish. To those being saved, it is God’s very power.
Paul quotes Isaiah: God promised to overturn the self-assured wisdom of the worldly wise.

f.w: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise

n: Where are the philosophers, the legal scholars, and the clever debaters now? God has shown that the world’s wisdom cannot save.

f.g: A Jewish expert in the law of Moses.
A debater or philosopher who argues points for sport.

n: In God’s wise plan, human cleverness could never find God on its own. So He chose to save believers through preaching that the world calls foolish.

f.g: The seemingly foolish message preached — Christ crucified — not foolish preaching style.

n: Paul’s Jewish listeners wanted miraculous proof; his Greek listeners wanted impressive philosophy. Each audience had its own demand.
But Paul preaches a crucified Messiah. To Jews, a Messiah hung on a cross was offensive; to Greeks, worshiping an executed man seemed ridiculous.

f.g: Greek skandalon — something that trips people up or offends.

n: But for those who answer God’s call, whatever their background, Christ is both the power of God the Jews sought and the wisdom of God the Greeks sought.
Even what looks like foolishness or weakness in God surpasses humanity’s greatest wisdom and strength. Paul uses irony to make the point.

f.w: the weakness of God is stronger than men

n: Paul invites them to look at their own congregation: not many were educated, powerful, or from noble families by worldly standards.

f.g: By human, worldly standards.

n: God deliberately chose the humble and weak to shame those who think themselves wise and strong. His work doesn’t depend on worldly status.

f.w: the weak things of the world

n: He even chose the lowly, the despised, and the “nobodies” to bring to nothing what the world considers important.

f.g: Lowly things, of low birth or status.
People counted as nothing in society.

n: The purpose: no human being can boast before God. Salvation is His gift, not our achievement.

f.g: Here, to boast or brag.

n: It is God who placed them in Christ, and Christ becomes everything they need: true wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.

f.g: Release purchased by a price — like freeing a slave or prisoner.

n: Paul quotes Jeremiah: if anyone wants to boast, let them boast about the Lord and what He has done.

f.w: He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord
